name: Ashpile HandStitch Thermal Wrap Layer
description:
A thick, irregular underlayer stitched together from salvaged fleece offcuts, industrial insulation batting, and torn synthetic jersey. Seams are visible and mismatched — some double-stitched with wire thread, others sealed with heat-bond tape. Colors range from ash-gray to oil-stained beige, with dark patches where material sources changed mid-construction. No two are identical.

Common across Shelf settlements near the lake corridor where acid-rain wind cuts through rusted wall gaps at night. Worn under scavenged coats, the bulk shows at the collar and wrists — a clear marker of Shelf survival.
functionality: Provides basic passive insulation against cold and acid-damp. No active systems. Layered construction traps body heat in uneven pockets. Rough inner surface chafes on bare skin — most wearers add a thin cotton slip beneath.
what_it_says: You made this yourself, or someone who cares about you did — survival sewn by hand.
story_hooks: A specific stitch pattern identifies this layer as made by a known Shelf seamstress — her work turns up on bodies sometimes, and someone is counting.
Embedded inside the batting: a folded paper with a partial map of a Circuit-level maintenance tunnel entry point.
The heat-bond tape along the left side is partially peeled — underneath is a different fabric entirely, one that doesn't match anything sold in M88.
